Yes — you have several realistic options that cost nothing or almost nothing, and Switzerland has a specific mechanism where the state pays for a lawyer if you need one. Here's the practical route:

**Who to go to first**

1. **Unia** (trade union), Region Zentralschweiz, office in Lucerne. Initial advice is free; membership fees are income-scaled and low, and members get full legal support. Wage recovery in the cleaning sector is Unia's bread and butter — a union letter alone often shakes money loose. (VPOD or Syna are alternatives depending on your employer.)
2. **KAA – Kompetenzzentrum Arbeit und Arbeitsmarkt** (joint body of the cleaning industry, based in Bern). Many cleaning companies are bound by the national collective agreement (**L-GAV Reinigungsgewerbe**). The KAA can tell you if yours is — if so, you may be covered by sector minimum wages (you might be owed *more* than 7,800), and there's a **wage guarantee fund** that pays out if the employer goes bankrupt (within limits, with deadlines — so don't wait).

Both can help you sequence the steps below.

**Cheap self-help you can start today**

- Send a written payment reminder (**Mahnung**) by registered mail (**Einschreiben**) with a ~10-day deadline. Keep a copy.
- Gather evidence: employment contract, **time sheets**, payslips, schedules, messages, witnesses.
- If the deadline passes, you can file a **Zahlungsbefehl** (payment order) yourself at the **Betreibungs- und Konkursamt (BEKO)** in Lucerne — one office for the whole canton. Cost roughly CHF 100–200, and if you're on social assistance you can ask about a fee waiver. No lawyer needed for this step.
- If the employer doesn't object, the office can push the company into bankruptcy. If it objects (**Rechtsvorschlag**), a lawsuit would be needed — see below. Important: wage claims from the **last six months rank first in a bankruptcy** (Art. 219 SchKG), so your 7,800 is protected territory — but move fast if the firm looks shaky. You can also claim **5% default interest**.

**The state help with costs: unentgeltliche Rechtspflege**

If a court case becomes necessary, apply for **free legal aid** at the court. If your income and assets are low (you'll submit a simple budget with proof) and your case isn't hopeless, the canton covers court fees **and appoints a lawyer at no cost to you**. Forms are on the Lucerne courts' website; Unia, KAA, or social services can help you fill them in. In Lucerne, employment disputes normally go through a conciliation hearing at the **Friedensgericht** first, then to the **Bezirksgericht**.

**Money to live on in the meantime**

- **Sozialhilfe**: apply at your commune's social service (*Sozialdienst*) **now**, before your savings run out — not after. Having unpaid wage claims pending doesn't disqualify you.
- If the job ends: register with the **RAV** (regional employment office) immediately so you don't lose unemployment benefits.

**Small but useful points**

- Lucerne no longer has a workers' ombudsman office (it was abolished years ago) — don't waste time looking for one.
- Don't sign any waiver, "voluntary resignation," or settlement under pressure, and don't accept vague promises of cash later — get everything in writing.
- Keep working and documenting your hours unless advised otherwise; if they tell you to stop coming in, write down the date — wages may still be owed.
- A new federal insolvency wage-protection scheme (Art. 219a SchKG) is being phased in from 2026 — worth checking its current status when you act.

If you can find out whether your employer belongs to the industry association or is bound by the L-GAV, the advice can be narrowed down further — the KAA can confirm that with one call.

Yes — you can do a lot in Switzerland without paying a lawyer up front, and there are two routes designed exactly for people in your situation.

**Who to go to first**

1. **Unia** (trade union), Region Zentralschweiz, office in Lucerne. Initial advice is free; membership fees are income-scaled and low, and members get full legal support. Wage recovery in the cleaning sector is Unia's bread and butter; a union letter alone often shakes money loose.
2. **KAA – Kompetenzzentrum Arbeit und Arbeitsmarkt** (joint body of the cleaning industry, Bern). Most cleaning companies are bound by the national collective agreement (L-GAV Reinigungsgewerbe). The KAA can tell you whether yours is; if so you may be covered by sector minimum wages (you might be owed more than 7,800), a conciliation procedure, and — crucially — a **wage guarantee fund** that pays outstanding wages if the employer goes bankrupt.

Both will also help you decide the order of the steps below.

**Cheap self-help you can start today**

- Send a **Mahnung** (written payment reminder) by registered mail (Einschreiben), setting a deadline of ~10 days. Keep a copy.
- Gather evidence: employment contract, **time sheets/working records**, payslips, work schedules, messages, names of witnesses.
- If the deadline passes, file a **Zahlungsbefehl** (payment order) yourself at the **Betreibungs- und Konkursamt (BEKO)** in Lucerne — it's the one office for the whole canton. Cost roughly CHF 100–200; if you're on social assistance ask about a fee waiver. You don't need a lawyer for this.
- If the employer doesn't object, the debt office can push the company into bankruptcy; if it does object (Rechtsvorschlag), you'd need a lawsuit — see next point. Note wage claims from the **last 6 months rank first** in a bankruptcy (Art. 219 SchKG), so your 7,800 is well within the protected amount — but move fast if the firm looks shaky.
- You can also claim **5% default interest**.

**The state help with legal costs: unentgeltliche Rechtspflege**

If a court case becomes necessary, apply for **free legal aid** at the court. If your income/assets are low (they'll ask for a simple budget + proofs) and your case isn't hopeless, the canton pays the court fees and appoints a lawyer at no cost to you. Forms are on the Lucerne courts' website; Unia, KAA or social services can help you fill them in. In Lucerne, employment disputes normally start with a conciliation hearing at the **Friedensgericht** before the main case goes to the **Bezirksgericht**.

**Money to live on in the meantime**

- **Sozialhilfe**: apply at your commune's social service (Sozialdienst) now, before you're out of funds — not after. Declare the unpaid wages; that doesn't disqualify you.
- If the job ends: register with the **RAV** (regional employment office) immediately so you don't lose unemployment benefits.

**Small but useful**

- Lucerne no longer has a workers' ombudsman office (abolished years ago) — don't waste time looking.
- Don't sign any "waiver," resignation or settlement under pressure; don't accept vague promises of cash later — get everything in writing.
- Keep working and documenting your hours unless advised otherwise; if they tell you to stop coming, note the date — wages may still be owed.
- A new federal wage-protection scheme for employer insolvencies (Art. 219a SchKG) is being phased in from 2026; check whether it already applies when you act.
